title: What can add across a C=C bond? Hydrogen, halogens, hydrogen halides and water, with their conditions
subtitle: Hydrogen can add across the double bonds in vegetable oil and turn it solid. What else can add across a C=C bond, under what conditions, and what product does each make?
subject: Chemistry
lessonIntent: explaining why an alkene can add and an alkane cannot; writing equations with structural formulas and conditions on the arrow for an alkene with H₂, X₂, HX and H₂O; naming the haloalkane and alcohol products; recognising when an unsymmetrical alkene gives two possible products. No alkane substitution or alkyne addition (chem-m7-c04b), no test method or limits (chem-m7-p02), no Markovnikov's rule.

voiceover.text: Vegetable oil is a liquid, and its long molecules contain carbon to carbon double bonds. Add hydrogen gas, with a nickel catalyst and heat, and the hydrogen adds across some of those double bonds. The oil turns into a soft solid. For much of the last century, that's how margarine was made. Hydrogen isn't the only thing that can add to a double bond, though. So what can add across a C double bond C, and what does it make?

Start with why. In an alkane, every carbon already has four single bonds, so there's no spare bond for a new atom. It's saturated. An alkene's double bond is different. As you saw in the properties video, its second bond is the weaker one, and its electrons sit above and below the carbons, where other molecules can reach them. That second bond can break. Then each carbon has one spare bond, and a new atom can join each one.

That's an addition reaction: two molecules join to make one, and no atoms are lost. Picture the reagent, the molecule being added, splitting in two, with one piece on each carbon of the old double bond. Afterwards those carbons have only single bonds, so they change from flat to tetrahedral. Alkanes have no double bond to open, so they react in a different way, which is the next video.

Now the four reagents, one at a time. First, hydrogen. Ethene plus H two gives ethane, with one hydrogen on each carbon. The product has no double bond left, so it's saturated. Hydrogen barely reacts on its own, so it needs a nickel catalyst and heat, about one hundred and fifty degrees, and we write those conditions on the arrow. From Module five, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so it goes on the arrow, not in the equation. This is hydrogenation, the reaction that hardens vegetable oil.

Second, a halogen, X two, such as bromine or chlorine. Ethene plus bromine puts one bromine on each carbon. A halogen in a name works like a branch: a prefix with a number. So this is one, two-dibromoethane. Chlorine works the same way, giving one, two-dichloroethane. No catalyst is needed, and it's fast at room temperature. Bromine water is orange because of the bromine in it. When an alkene adds that bromine, the colour disappears. That makes it a quick test for a double bond, which you'll carry out in the practical video.

Third, a hydrogen halide, H X, such as hydrogen bromide or hydrogen chloride. This time the two pieces are different: the hydrogen goes to one carbon, and the bromine to the other. Ethene gives bromoethane. It needs no number, because both carbons in ethane are alike. With hydrogen chloride, you'd get chloroethane. This one also works at room temperature, with no catalyst.

Fourth, water. The pieces are H and O H. Ethene and water give ethanol, with the O H on one carbon and the H on the other. Hydration needs the most conditions: steam, an acid catalyst such as phosphoric acid, about three hundred degrees for a fast enough rate, and high pressure. Why the pressure? The reaction is an equilibrium, and two gas molecules become one. From Module five, raising the pressure shifts an equilibrium towards fewer gas molecules, so towards ethanol. This is one industrial route to ethanol.

Ethene is the same at both ends, so it gives just one product. Propene isn't. When hydrogen bromide adds to propene, the bromine can land on the end carbon, or on the middle carbon of the old double bond. So there are two possible products: one-bromopropane and two-bromopropane. In an answer, write both. Water does the same, giving propan-one-ol or propan-two-ol. A symmetrical alkene, like but-two-ene, gives only one product, whichever way round the pieces add.

So check every addition equation the same way. Two reactants make one product, and every atom of the reagent ends up on the two old double-bond carbons. Count them: two carbons, four hydrogens and two bromines on each side. If you write HBr as a second product, you've swapped a bromine in for a hydrogen. That's substitution, not addition.

So, four reagents, one pattern. Split the reagent, and put one piece on each carbon: H and H, X and X, H and X, or H and O H. Then match the conditions: nickel and heat for hydrogen, room temperature for halogens and hydrogen halides, and acid, heat and pressure for water.
Your turn. Propene reacts with chlorine at room temperature. Write a balanced equation for this reaction using structural formulas, and name the organic product. Pause here to answer.

Chlorine adds across the double bond, with one chlorine on each carbon of the old C double bond C. The product is C H three, C H Cl, C H two Cl: one, two-dichloropropane. There's only one product, because both pieces are the same. Writing H Cl as a second product would be substitution. In an addition, nothing is lost.

Last one. Compound X has the formula C four H eight, and it decolourises bromine water rapidly. When X reacts with steam, using a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure, only one alcohol product is possible. Identify X, and justify your answer. Pause here to answer.

Decolourising bromine water shows a double bond, so X isn't a ring like cyclobutane. Three alkenes are C four H eight. But-one-ene and two-methylpropene are different at each end, so water can add either way round, giving two possible alcohols. But-two-ene is symmetrical, so it gives only butan-two-ol. So X is but-two-ene. But-one-ene doesn't fit, because it can give two alcohols.

So anything that splits into two pieces, H two, X two, H X or water, can add across a double bond. But what about alkanes, with no double bond to open? And alkynes, with a triple bond? Next: why alkanes substitute, while alkenes and alkynes add.
